title: Plant Hardiness Zone: USDA Zones by Location
description: Find the USDA plant hardiness zone for any location with the Plant Hardiness Zone finder — 2023 map basis, half-zones included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Chicago gardens sit in zone 6a on the 2023 USDA map, where average winter lows reach −10 to −5 °F (−23.3 to −20.6 °C) — the number printed on every seed packet sold there.
quick_answer: The Plant Hardiness Zone finder tells you the USDA hardiness zone of any location — the band based on the average coldest winter temperature, which decides which perennial plants survive outdoors there. Enter the place and read its zone and half-zone — the code printed on plant labels.
steps_intro: One winter number decides what survives:

body.t: A shrub rated 'zones 5–8' is a promise about winter cold. Check your zone before the nursery run and the promise becomes testable — gardeners in zone 6a buy differently from zone 8a.
Relocating gardeners bring habits from the old zone. The new zone recalibrates what 'hardy' means before the first beloved plant dies learning it.
The 2023 USDA revision (1991–2020 data) moved roughly half the US map about half a zone warmer than 2012. Your zone from memory may be a zone out of date.
Trees are decades-long bets placed on winter minima. Zone first, cultivar second — with microclimate judgement layered on top, as the FAQs insist.

Zone 6b means the average annual extreme minimum winter temperature is −5 to 0 °F (−20.6 to −17.8 °C). Not the coldest ever recorded — the average of each year's coldest night across three decades. Plants rated to zone 6 survive the typical worst night, not the legendary one.

body.t: Minneapolis moved from 4b on the 2012 map to about 5a on the 2023 map — winters' coldest nights averaged roughly 5 °F warmer in the newer data window. Gardeners there felt it before the map admitted it.

popular_table.title: USDA zones — winter minimum bands
popular_table.intro: Each full zone spans 10 °F of average annual extreme minimum temperature; half-zones (a/b) split it into 5 °F steps.
popular_table.note: The 2023 USDA map (based on 1991–2020 data from thousands of weather stations) is the current edition. Britain and Europe use their own hardiness framings — RHS ratings and European zone adaptations echo the same idea.

faq: Does the zone use the coldest night ever?

No — it averages the single coldest night of each winter across the data period. A once-in-50-years freeze goes below the zone's floor; that is why experienced gardeners near a boundary buy half a zone of margin.

Often true: south walls, city heat islands, cold-air drainage and snow cover shift a garden's reality by half a zone or more either way. The map gives the regional baseline; your thermometer keeps the local truth.
Correct — heat, humidity, rainfall and season length are separate axes (heat-zone maps exist for the first). Two zone-7 gardens, coastal Oregon and inland Georgia, garden very differently.

Canada publishes its own hardiness map on a related but distinct formula; Europe is often described with USDA-equivalent zones in catalogues. This page speaks the USDA system named on North American labels.
Pots expose roots to far colder temperatures than the ground feels — treat container plants as needing roughly two zones of extra hardiness, the nurseryman's rule of thumb.
How often does the map change?
USDA revised in 2012 and 2023 as data windows roll forward. Zones are climate statistics, not borders — expect slow drift, and re-check before big plantings.
Reliably: snow is insulation, and perennials under a steady snowpack survive air temperatures well below their rating. The zone counts air temperature only — one more reason locals out-garden maps.
Different data (spring/autumn averages) and just as decision-relevant for annuals — zones govern perennial survival through winter, frost dates govern the growing season's bookends.
